scope: Frozen initial Reliability, excluding all APRL regardless of subsequent classification

document.name: revcl-ActiveDirectoryWindowsServer
document.title: When deploying Active Directory on Windows Server, use a location with Availability Zones and deploy at least two VMs across these zones. If not available, deploy in an Availability Set

document.name: revcl-AzureApplicationConsistentSnapshotToolAzureNetappFiles
document.title: If you deploy Azure NetApp Files for your HANA, Oracle, or DB2 database, use the Azure Application Consistent Snapshot tool (AzAcSnap) to take application-consistent snapshots. AzAcSnap also supports Oracle databases. Consider using AzAcSnap on a central VM rather than on individual VMs.

document.name: revcl-AzureAvailabilitySetAvailabilityZone
document.title: Before you deploy your high-availability infrastructure, and depending on the region you choose, determine whether to deploy with an Azure availability set or an availability zone.

document.name: revcl-AzureAvailabilitySetsAzureAvailabilityZone
document.title: You can't deploy Azure availability sets within an Azure availability zone unless you use proximity placement groups.

document.name: revcl-AzureBackupServiceHanaDatabase
document.title: Help protect your HANA database by using the Azure Backup service.

document.name: revcl-AzureDisasterRecoveryRegionsVpnConnections
document.title: Set up ExpressRoute connections from on-premises to the primary and secondary Azure disaster recovery regions. Also, as an alternative to using ExpressRoute, consider setting up VPN connections from on-premises to the primary and secondary Azure disaster recovery regions.

document.name: revcl-AzureNetappFilesPremiumManagedSsds
document.title: Run all production systems on Premium managed SSDs and use Azure NetApp Files or Ultra Disk Storage. At least the OS disk should be on the Premium tier so you can achieve better performance and the best SLA.

document.name: revcl-AzureProximityPlacementGroupsSameProximityPlacementGroup
document.title: When you use Azure proximity placement groups in an availability set deployment, all three SAP components (central services, application server, and database) should be in the same proximity placement group.

document.name: revcl-AzureSiteRecoveryHighAvailabilityConfiguration
document.title: Consider configuring high availability depending on the type of storage you use for your SAP workloads. Some storage services available in Azure are not supported by Azure Site Recovery, so your high availability configuration may differ.

document.name: revcl-AzureSiteRecoveryMonitoringDisasterRecoveryService
document.title: Use Azure Site Recovery monitoring to maintain the health of the disaster recovery service for SAP application servers.

document.name: revcl-CentralServicesClusterVmsLinuxPacemakerCluster
document.title: Use Site Recovery to replicate an application server to a DR site. Site Recovery can also help with replicating central-services cluster VMs to the DR site. When you invoke DR, you'll need to reconfigure the Linux Pacemaker cluster on the DR site (for example, replace the VIP or SBD, run corosync.conf, and more).

document.name: revcl-CloudAdaptionFrameworkResiliencyReport
document.title: Run the Resiliency Report to ensure that the configuration of the entire provisioned Azure infrastructure (Compute, Database, Networking, Storage, Site Recovery) complies with the configuration defined by Cloud Adaption Framework for Azure.

document.name: revcl-CommonArchitecturePatternDifferentStorageStacks
document.title: Azure doesn't support architectures in which the primary and secondary VMs share storage for DBMS data. For the DBMS layer, the common architecture pattern is to replicate databases at the same time and with different storage stacks than the ones that the primary and secondary VMs use.

document.name: revcl-CrossRegionReplicationAzure
document.title: Consider cross-region replication in Azure for BCDR with paired regions

document.name: revcl-DifferentAvailabilityZonesHighAvailability
document.title: Follow VM rules for high availability on the VM level (premium disks, two or more in a region, in different availability zones)

document.name: revcl-DifferentNativeAzureStorageServicesRespectiveStorageService
document.title: Different native Azure storage services (like Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files, Azure Shared Disk) may not be available in all regions. So to have similar SAP setup on the DR region after failover, ensure the respective storage service is offered in DR site.

document.name: revcl-DirectorySynchronizationReplication
document.title: Don't replicate! Replication can create issues with directory synchronization

document.name: revcl-FiveDifferentCentralServicesDifferentApplicationServices
document.title: Don't group different application services in the same cluster. For example, don't combine DRBD and central services clusters on the same cluster. However, you can use the same Pacemaker cluster to manage approximately five different central services (multi-SID cluster).

document.name: revcl-FloatingIpLoadBalancer
document.title: Make sure the Floating IP is enabled on the Load balancer

document.name: revcl-GeoDisasterRecoveryCapabilitiesLocalizedResourceCapacityConstraint
document.title: Consider a multi-region deployment. Depending on customer size, locations, and users presence, operating in multiple regions can be a common choice to deliver services and run applications closer to them. Using a multi-region deployment is also important to provide geo disaster recovery capabilities, to eliminate the dependency from a single region capacity and diminish the risk of a temporary and localized resource capacity constraint

document.name: revcl-GlobalScaleCloudPlatformRightAzureRegionS
document.title: Select the right Azure region/s for your deployment. Azure is a global-scale cloud platform that provide global coverage through many regions and geographies. Different Azure regions have different characteristics, access and availability models, costs, capacity, and services offered, then it is important to consider all criteria and requirements

document.name: revcl-GlobalVnetPeeringMultipleAzureRegions
document.title: Local and global VNet peering provide connectivity and are the preferred approaches to ensure connectivity between landing zones for SAP deployments across multiple Azure regions

document.name: revcl-KeyVaultContentsDrRegion
document.title: Replicate key vault contents like certificates, secrets, or keys across regions so you can decrypt data in the DR region.

document.name: revcl-MicrosoftEntraConnectStagingSever
document.title: When deploying Microsoft Entra Connect, leverage a staging sever for high availability / Disaster recovery

document.name: revcl-MultipleIdentiyProvidersFacebookAccounts
document.title: Have multiple identiy providers (i.e., login with your microsoft, google, facebook accounts)

document.name: revcl-MultiRegions
document.title: Have active-active for multi-regions

document.name: revcl-NativeDatabaseReplicationTechnologyHaPair
document.title: Native database replication technology should be used to synchronize the database in a HA pair.

document.name: revcl-OneProximityPlacementGroupSapSid
document.title: Use one proximity placement group per SAP SID. Groups don't span across Availability Zones or Azure regions

document.name: revcl-PotentialPhysicalHardwareFailuresAzurePlannedMaintenance
document.title: When you create availability sets, use the maximum number of fault domains and update domains available. For example, if you deploy more than two VMs in one availability set, use the maximum number of fault domains (three) and enough update domains to limit the effect of potential physical hardware failures, network outages, or power interruptions, in addition to Azure planned maintenance. The default number of fault domains is two, and you can't change it online later.

document.name: revcl-PrimaryVirtualNetworkDrSite
document.title: The CIDR for the primary virtual network (VNet) shouldn't conflict or overlap with the CIDR of the DR site's VNet

document.name: revcl-RecoveryTimesRtoRequirements
document.title: Test the backup and recovery times to verify that they meet your RTO requirements for restoring all systems simultaneously after a disaster.

document.name: revcl-RequiredServicesDeploymentRegions-1
document.title: Ensure required services and features are available within the chosen deployment regions

document.name: revcl-SameAvailabilitySetCentralServicesVms
document.title: Do not mix servers of different roles in the same availability set. Keep central services VMs, database VMs, application VMs in their own availability sets

document.name: revcl-SameHighAvailabilityClusterRedHatEnterpriseLinux
document.title: Azure supports installing and configuring SAP HANA and ASCS/SCS and ERS instances on the same high availability cluster running on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL).

document.name: revcl-SameHighAvailabilityOptionsAvailabilitySets
document.title: If you want to meet the infrastructure SLAs for your applications for SAP components (central services, application servers, and databases), you must choose the same high availability options (VMs, availability sets, availability zones) for all components.

document.name: revcl-SameLinuxPacemakerClusterFiveMultipleCentralServicesClusters
document.title: Azure doesn't currently support combining ASCS and DB HA in the same Linux Pacemaker cluster; separate them into individual clusters. However, you can combine up to five multiple central-services clusters into a pair of VMs.

document.name: revcl-SameStorageConfigurationSameSize
document.title: Deploy both VMs in the high-availability pair in an availability set or in availability zones. These VMs should be the same size and have the same storage configuration.

document.name: revcl-SapApplicationLayerComponentsSpecificHighAvailabilityScenarios
document.title: You can use Azure shared disks in Windows for ASCS + SCS components and specific high-availability scenarios. Set up your failover clusters separately for SAP application layer components and the DBMS layer. Azure doesn't currently support high-availability architectures that combine SAP application layer components and the DBMS layer into one failover cluster.

document.name: revcl-SapApplicationLayerComponentsStandardLoadBalancerSku
document.title: Most failover clusters for SAP application layer components (ASCS) and the DBMS layer require a virtual IP address for a failover cluster.  Azure Load Balancer should handle the virtual IP address for all other cases. One design principle is to use one load balancer per cluster configuration. We recommend that you use the standard version of the load balancer (Standard Load Balancer SKU).

document.name: revcl-SapApplicationServersAzureAvailabilityZones
document.title: When using Azure Availability Zones to achieve high availability, you must consider latency between SAP application servers and database servers. For zones with high latencies, operational procedures need to be in place to ensure that SAP application servers and database servers are running in the same zone at all times.

document.name: revcl-SapCentralServicesClustersOperatingSystem
document.title: Use one of the following services to run SAP central services clusters, depending on the operating system.

document.name: revcl-SapHanaDbVirtualNetworkDisasterRecoveryVirtualNetworks
document.title: Peer the primary and disaster recovery virtual networks. For example, for HANA System Replication, an SAP HANA DB virtual network needs to be peered to the disaster recovery site's SAP HANA DB virtual network.

document.name: revcl-SapHanaSystemReplicationSapApplicationLayer
document.title: You can replicate standard storage between paired regions, but you can't use standard storage to store your databases or virtual hard disks. You can replicate backups only between paired regions that you use. For all your other data, run your replication by using native DBMS features like SQL Server Always On or SAP HANA System Replication. Use a combination of Site Recovery, rsync or robocopy, and other third-party software for the SAP application layer.

document.name: revcl-SapSHanaArchitecturesSapWebDispatcher
document.title: Consider the availability of SAP software against single points of failure. This includes single points of failure within applications such as DBMSs utilized in SAP NetWeaver and SAP S/4HANA architectures, SAP ABAP and ASCS + SCS. Also, other tools such as SAP Web Dispatcher.

document.name: revcl-TimeRecoveryProductionDatabases
document.title: Perform a point-in-time recovery for your production databases at any point and in a time frame that meets your RTO; point-in-time recovery typically includes operator errors deleting data either on the DBMS layer or through SAP, incidentally

document.name: revcl-TransactionRedoLogFilesAzureNetappFiles
document.title: The DBMS data and transaction/redo log files are stored in Azure supported block storage or Azure NetApp Files. Azure Files or Azure Premium Files isn't supported as storage for DBMS data and/or redo log files with SAP workload.

document.name: revcl-TwoAzureNetappFilesAccountsAzureNetappFilesStorage
document.title: If you use Azure NetApp Files storage for your SAP deployments, at a minimum, create two Azure NetApp Files accounts in the Premium tier, in two regions.

document.name: revcl-UserFlowsResilientInterfaces
document.title: Make sure that your sign-in user flows are backed up and resilient. Make sure that the code that you use to sign-in your users are backed up and recoverable. Resilient interfaces with external processes

document.name: revcl-VeritasInfoscaleSupportFailoverWindowsServerFailoverClustering
document.title: For SAP and SAP databases, consider implementing automatic failover clusters. In Windows, Windows Server Failover Clustering supports failover. In Linux, Linux Pacemaker or third-party tools like SIOS Protection Suite and Veritas InfoScale support failover.

document.name: revcl-WriteAcceleratorFileSystem
document.title: You should run SAP HANA on Azure only on the types of storage that are certified by SAP. Note that certain volumes must be run on certain disk configurations, where applicable. These configurations include enabling Write Accelerator and using Premium storage. You also need to ensure that the file system that runs on storage is compatible with the DBMS that runs on the machine.

document.name: revcl-AzureAdDomainServiceStampsAdditionalRegions
document.title: Add Azure AD Domain service stamps to additional regions and locations

document.name: revcl-MicrosoftIdentityLibraryLiveRevocableToken
document.title: Use long-live revocable token, cache your token and acquire your silently using Microsoft Identity Library

document.name: revcl-ReplicaSetsDr
document.title: Use Replica Sets for DR

document.name: revcl-ApimLimits
document.title: Be aware of APIM's limits

document.name: revcl-AutomatedBackupRoutine
document.title: Ensure there is an automated backup routine

document.name: revcl-MultiRegionModelRegionalBackends
document.title: In multi-region model, use Policies to route the requests to regional backends based on availability or latency.

document.name: revcl-OneUnitAvailabilityZones
document.title: Deploy at least one unit in two or more availability zones for an increased SLA of 99.99%

document.name: revcl-OverBackendUrlFailingCalls
document.title: Use Policies to add a fail-over backend URL and caching to reduce failing calls.

document.name: revcl-PremiumTierDr
document.title: For DR, leverage the premium tier with deployments scaled across two or more regions for 99.99% SLA

document.name: revcl-PremiumTierProductionWorkloads
document.title: Use the premium tier for production workloads.

document.name: revcl-SelfHostedGatewayDeployments
document.title: Ensure that the self-hosted gateway deployments are resilient.

document.name: revcl-ActivePassiveApplicationGuidanceCrossRegionDr
document.title: For cross-region DR, deploy container apps in multiple regions and follow active/active or active/passive application guidance.

document.name: revcl-FrontDoorClosestRegion
document.title: Use Front Door or Traffic Manager to route traffic to the closest region

document.name: revcl-LeverageAvailabilityZones
document.title: Leverage Availability Zones if regionally applicable

document.name: revcl-OneReplicaZoneRedundancy
document.title: Use more than one replica and enable Zone Redundancy.

document.name: revcl-AppInstanceApps
document.title: Use more than 1 app instance for your apps

document.name: revcl-AzureSpringAppsApplicationInsights
document.title: Monitor Azure Spring Apps with logs, metrics and tracing. Integrate ASA with application insights and track failures and create workbooks.

document.name: revcl-AzureSpringAppsAvailabilityZones
document.title: In supported region, Azure Spring Apps can be deployed as zone redundant, which means that instances are automatically distributed across availability zones. This feature is only available in Standard and Enterprise tiers.

document.name: revcl-AzureSpringAppsInstancesMultipleRegions
document.title: Azure Spring Apps instances could be created in multiple regions for your applications and traffic could be routed by Traffic Manager/Front Door.

document.name: revcl-BlueGreenDeploymentStrategiesAzureSpringApps
document.title: Azure Spring Apps permits two deployments for every app, only one of which receives production traffic. You can achieve zero downtime with blue green deployment strategies. Blue green deployment is only available in Standard and Enterprise tiers. You could automate deployment using CI/CD with ADO/GitHub actions

document.name: revcl-MissionCriticalAppsEnterprisePlan
document.title: Use Enterprise plan for commercial support of spring boot for mission critical apps. With other tiers you get OSS support.

document.name: revcl-SpringCloudGateway
document.title: Set up autoscaling in Spring Cloud Gateway

document.name: revcl-StandardConsumptionDedicatedPlan
document.title: Enable autoscale for the apps with Standard consumption & dedicated plan.

document.name: revcl-AppropriateVsanDataRedundancyMethodRaidSpecification
document.title: Ensure that the appropriate vSAN Data redundancy method is used (RAID specification)

document.name: revcl-AutomatedRecoveryPlansDisasterSolutions
document.title: Use Automated recovery plans with either of the Disaster solutions, avoid manual tasks as much as possible

document.name: revcl-AzureNetappFilesAzureVmwareSolution
document.title: When Azure Netapp Files is used to extend storage for Azure VMware Solution,consider using this as a VMware datastore instead of attaching directly to a VM.

document.name: revcl-AzureVmwareSolutionPrivateCloudBackupSolution
document.title: Deploy your backup solution in the same region as your Azure VMware Solution private cloud

document.name: revcl-AzureVmwareSolutionPrivateCloudsExpressrouteGlobalReach
document.title: Will ExpressRoute Global Reach be used for connectivity between the primary and secondary Azure VMware Solution Private Clouds or is routing done through network virtual appliances?

document.name: revcl-BackupSolutionNativeComponents
document.title: Deploy your backup solution outside of vSan, on Azure native components

document.name: revcl-BackupSolutionsBusiness
document.title: Have all Backup solutions been considered and a solution that is best for your business been decided upon? [ MABS/CommVault/Metallic.io/Veeam/ï¿½. ]

document.name: revcl-DifferentAddressSpacesDifferentRegions
document.title: Use 2 different address spaces between the regions, for example: 10.0.0.0/16 and 192.168.0.0/16 for the different regions

document.name: revcl-DisasterRecoveryRequirementEnoughQuota
document.title: Ensure that you have requested enough quota, ensuring you have considered growth and Disaster Recovery requirement

document.name: revcl-DisasterRecoverySolutionStretchedCluster
document.title: If using stretched cluster, ensure that your selected Disaster Recovery solution is supported by the vendor

document.name: revcl-DisasterRecoveryTechnologyAzureSiteRecovery
document.title: Use Azure Site Recovery when the Disaster Recovery technology is native Azure IaaS

document.name: revcl-DrSolutionsBusiness
document.title: Have all DR solutions been considered and a solution that is best for your business been decided upon? [SRM/JetStream/Zerto/Veeam/...]

document.name: revcl-ExternalDataStorageSolutionsDedicatedExpressrouteGateway
document.title: Ensure that a dedicated ExpressRoute Gateway is being used for external data storage solutions

document.name: revcl-ExternalDataStorageSolutionsExpressrouteGateway
document.title: Ensure that FastPath is enabled on the ExpressRoute Gateway that is being used for external data storage solutions

document.name: revcl-FiniteResourceBackups
document.title: Ensure backups are not stored on vSAN as vSAN is a finite resource

document.name: revcl-LargerApplianceMonLimit
document.title: When using MON, be aware of the limits of simulataneously configured VMs (MON Limit for HCX [400 - standard, 1000 - Larger appliance])

document.name: revcl-NetworkExtensionsMon
document.title: When using MON, you cannot enable MON on more than 100 Network extensions

document.name: revcl-PremisesApplianceCloudAppliance
document.title: Ensure that migrations are started from the on-premises appliance and NOT from the Cloud appliance (do NOT perform a reverse migration)

document.name: revcl-SecondaryDisasterRecoveryEnvironmentGeopoliticalRegionPair
document.title: Use the geopolitical region pair as the secondary disaster recovery environment

document.name: revcl-SiteDisasterToleranceSettingsBusiness
document.title: Have site disaster tolerance settings been properly considered and changed for your business if needed.

document.name: revcl-StretchedClusterExpressrouteCircuits-1
document.title: If using stretched cluster, ensure that both ExpressRoute circuits have GlobalReach enabled.

document.name: revcl-StretchedClusterExpressrouteCircuits
document.title: If using stretched cluster, ensure that both ExpressRoute circuits are connected to your connectivity hub.

document.name: revcl-StretchedClusterSla
document.title: If using stretched cluster, ensure that the SLA provided will meet your requirements

document.name: revcl-VmwareComponentsAzurePlatform
document.title: Is a process in place to request a restore of the VMware components managed by the Azure Platform?

document.name: revcl-VsanStorageNeedsToleratePolicy
document.title: Ensure that the Failure-to-tolerate policy is in place to meet your vSAN storage needs

document.name: revcl-EuBotRegionalServiceAzureBotService
document.title: Azure Bot Service runs in active-active mode for both global and regional services. When an outage occurs, you don't need to detect errors or manage the service. Azure Bot Service automatically performs auto failover and auto recovery in a multi-region geographical architecture. For the EU bot regional service, Azure Bot Service provides two full regions inside Europe with active/active replication to ensure redundancy. For the global bot service, all available regions/geographies can be served as the global footprint.

document.name: revcl-LocalDataResidencyRegionalCompliance
document.title: Deploying bots with local data residency and regional compliance

document.name: revcl-ReliabilitySupportRecommendationsAzureBotService
document.title: Follow reliability support recommendations in Azure Bot Service

document.name: revcl-AzureCacheRedisInstance
document.title: Configure data persistence for an Azure Cache for Redis instance. Because your cache data is stored in memory, a rare and unplanned failure of multiple nodes can cause all the data to be dropped. To avoid losing data completely, Redis persistence allows you to take periodic snapshots of in-memory data, and store it to your storage account.

document.name: revcl-DifferentAzureAvailabilityZonesZoneRedundantCache
document.title: Enable zone redundancy for Azure Cache for Redis. Azure Cache for Redis supports zone redundant configurations in the Premium and Enterprise tiers. A zone redundant cache can place its nodes across different Azure Availability Zones in the same region. It eliminates data center or AZ outage as a single point of failure and increases the overall availability of your cache.

document.name: revcl-GeoRedundantStorageAccountAzureCache
document.title: Use Geo-redundant storage account to persist Azure Cache for Redis data, or zonally redundant where geo-redundancy is not available

document.name: revcl-TwoPremiumTierCacheInstancesPremiumAzureCache
document.title: Configure passive geo-replication for Premium Azure Cache for Redis instances. Geo-replication is a mechanism for linking two or more Azure Cache for Redis instances, typically spanning two Azure regions. Geo-replication is designed mainly for cross-region disaster recovery. Two Premium tier cache instances are connected through geo-replication in a way that provides reads and writes to your primary cache, and that data is replicated to the secondary cache.

document.title: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery (BCDR) considerations with Azure OpenAI Service

document.title: Backup Your ChatGPT conversations

document.name: revcl-CustomSpeechCiCd
document.title: CI/CD for custom speech

document.name: revcl-KnowledgeBaseExportImport
document.title: Move a knowledge base using export-import

document.name: revcl-LeverageFtaHandbookCognitiveServices
document.title: Leverage FTA HandBook for Cognitive Services

document.name: revcl-Prompts
document.title: Backup Your Prompts

document.name: wafsg-AppropriateDeploymentOptionUseCase
document.title: Resiliency: Choose the appropriate deployment option of either pay-as-you-go or provisioned throughput based on your use case. Because reserved capacity increases resiliency, choose provisioned throughput for production solutions. The pay-as-you-go approach is ideal for dev/test environments.

document.name: wafsg-AzureBlobStoreLargeDataFiles
document.title: Resiliency: Follow the guidance for large data files and import the data from an Azure blob store. Large files, 100 MB or larger, can become unstable when uploaded through multipart forms because the requests are atomic and can't be retried or resumed.

document.name: wafsg-CapacityUsageThroughputLimits
document.title: Resiliency: Monitor capacity usage to ensure you aren't exceeding throughput limits. Regularly review capacity usage to achieve more accurate forecasting and help prevent service interruptions due to capacity constraints.

document.name: wafsg-ImportantThroughputInformationRateLimits
document.title: Monitor rate limits for pay-as-you-go: If you're using the pay-as-you-go approach, manage rate limits for your model deployments and monitor usage of tokens per minute (TPM) and requests per minute (RPM).
document.description: This important throughput information provides information required to ensure that you assign enough TPM from your quota to meet the demand for your deployments.Assigning enough quota prevents throttling of calls to your deployed models.

document.name: wafsg-MultipleAzureOpenaiInstancesAzureOpenaiDeployments
document.title: Redundancy: Add the appropriate gateways in front of your Azure OpenAI deployments. The gateway must have the capability to withstand transient failures like throttling and also route to multiple Azure OpenAI instances. Consider routing to instances in different regions to build regional redundancy.

document.name: wafsg-OpaqueRiskAnalysisTuneContentFilters
document.title: Tune content filters: Tune content filters to minimize false positives from overly aggressive filters.
document.description: Content filters block prompts or completions based on an opaque risk analysis. Ensure content filters are tuned to allow expected usage for your workload.

document.name: wafsg-ThroughputModelResiliency
document.title: Resiliency: If you're using provisioned throughput, consider also deploying a pay-as-you-go instance to handle overflow. You can route calls to the pay-as-you-go instance via your gateway when your provisioned throughput model is throttled. You can also use monitoring to predict when the model will be throttled and preemptively route calls to the pay-as-you-go instance.

document.name: wafsg-ThroughputPaymentModelProvisionedThroughput
document.title: Monitor provision-managed utilization for provisioned throughput: If you're using the provisioned throughput payment model, monitor provision-managed utilization.
document.description: It's important to monitor provision-managed utilization to ensure it doesn't exceed 100%, to prevent throttling of calls to your deployed models.

document.name: wafsg-TrainingDataAzureOpenai
document.title: Recovery: Define a recovery strategy that includes a recovery plan for models that are fine-tuned and for training data uploaded to Azure OpenAI. Because Azure OpenAI doesn't have automatic failover, you must design a strategy that encompasses the entire service and all dependencies, such as storage that contains training data.

document.name: revcl-AvailabilityZonesAvailabilitySets
document.title: For regions that do not support Availability Zones deploy VMs into Availability Sets
document.description: Use at least two VMs in Availability Sets to isolate VMs on different fault and update domains.

document.name: revcl-AzureLoadBalancerIncomingNetworkTraffic
document.title: Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway distribute incoming network traffic across multiple resources.

document.name: revcl-AzureMetadataServiceUpcomingMaintenanceEvents
document.title: Utilize Scheduled Events to prepare for VM maintenance
document.description: Scheduled Events is an Azure Metadata Service that provides information about upcoming maintenance events for virtual machines (VMs). By leveraging Scheduled Events, you can proactively prepare your applications for VM maintenance, minimizing disruption and improving the availability of your VMs.

document.name: revcl-AzureVirtualMachinesAzureBackup
document.title: Consider Azure Backup to meet your resiliency requirements for Azure VMs
document.description: Ensure that Azure Backup is utilized appropriately to meet your organization's resiliency requirements for Azure virtual machines (VMs).

document.name: revcl-LeverageAvailabilityZonesOtherAvailabilityZones
document.title: Leverage Availability Zones for your VMs in regions where they are supported
document.description: Co-locate your compute, storage, networking, and data resources across an availability zone, and replicate this arrangement in other availability zones.

document.name: revcl-LeverageAvailabilityZonesVms
document.title: Leverage Availability Zones for your VMs in regions where they are supported.

document.name: revcl-ManagedDisksDataDurability
document.title: Ensure Managed Disks are used for all VMs
document.description: Azure automatically replicates managed disks within a region to ensure data durability and protect against single-point failures.

document.name: revcl-NetworkVirtualAppliancesNecessaryNvaConfiguration
document.title: Deploy Network Virtual Appliances (NVAs) in a vendor supported configuration for High Availability
document.description: When choosing the best option for deploying NVAs in Azure, it is crucial to consider the vendor's recommendations and validate that the specific design has been vetted and validated by the NVA vendor. The vendor should also provide the necessary NVA configuration for seamless integration in Azure.

document.name: revcl-PartnerNetworkingTechnologiesPartnerVendor
document.title: When deploying partner networking technologies or NVAs, follow the partner vendor's guidance

document.name: revcl-PotentialResourceConstraintsDrRegion
document.title: Increase quotas in DR region before testing failover with ASR
document.description: By ensuring that the necessary quotas are increased in your DR region before testing failover with ASR, you can avoid any potential resource constraints during the recovery process for failed over VMs.

document.name: revcl-RecoveryTimeObjectiveLowRtoRequirements
document.title: For Azure and on-premises VMs (Hyper-V/Phyiscal/VMware) with low RTO requirements use Azure Site Recovery
document.description: Azure Site Recovery enables you to achieve low RTO (Recovery Time Objective) for your Azure and hybrid VMs by providing continuous replication and failover capabilities.

document.name: revcl-SqlServerTempdbTempDisk
document.title: Do not use the Temp disk for anything that is not acceptable to be lost
document.description: Temporary disks are intended for short-term storage of non-persistent data such as page files, swap files, or SQL Server tempdb. Storing persistent data on temporary disks can lead to data loss during maintenance events or VM redeployment.

document.name: revcl-UseCapacityReservationsCriticalWorkloads
document.title: Use Capacity Reservations for critical workloads that require guaranteed capacity
document.description: By using Capacity Reservations, you can effectively manage capacity for critical workloads, ensuring resource availability in specified regions.

document.name: revcl-VirtualMachineConnectivitySingleInstanceVms
document.title: Use Premium or Ultra disks for production VMs
document.description: Single Instance VMs using Premium SSD or Ultra Disk for all Operating System Disks and Data Disks are guaranteed to have Virtual Machine Connectivity of at least 99.9%

document.name: revcl-VirtualMachineScaleSetsAzureSiteRecovery
document.title: Avoid running a production workload on a single VM
document.description: Azure provides multiple options for VM redundancy to meet different requirements (Availability Zones, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Availability Sets, Azure Site Recovery)

document.name: wafsg-AutomaticRecoveryOptionsHealthDegradationMonitoring
document.title: Explore the automatic recovery options. Azure supports health degradation monitoring and self-healing features for VMs. For example, scale sets provide automatic instance repairs. In more advanced scenarios, self-healing involves using Azure Site Recovery, having a passive standby to fail over to, or redeploying from infrastructure as code (IaC). The method that you choose should align with the business requirements and your organizational operations. For more information, see VM service disruptions.

document.name: wafsg-CapacityReservationsFeatureApplicableSlas
document.title: (VMs) Take advantage of the capacity reservations feature.
document.description: Capacity is reserved for your use and is available within the scope of the applicable SLAs. You can delete capacity reservations when you no longer need them, and billing is consumption based.

document.name: wafsg-CompositeServiceLevelObjectivesAzureServiceLevelAgreements
document.title: Calculate your composite service-level objectives (SLOs) based on Azure service-level agreements (SLAs). Ensure that your SLO isn't higher than the Azure SLAs to avoid unrealistic expectations and potential issues.

document.name: wafsg-ComprehensiveDisasterRecoveryPlanComprehensivePlan
document.title: Create a comprehensive disaster recovery plan. Disaster preparedness involves creating a comprehensive plan and deciding on a technology for recovery.

document.name: wafsg-EphemeralOperatingSystemFailureModeAnalysis
document.title: Conduct a failure mode analysis to minimize points of failure by analyzing VM interactions with the network and storage components. Choose configurations like ephemeral operating system (OS) disks to localize disk access and avoid network hops. Add a load balancer to enhance self-preservation by distributing network traffic across multiple VMs, which improves availability and reliability.

document.name: wafsg-EphemeralOsDisksSeparateDataDisk
document.title: Create state isolation. Workload data should be on a separate data disk to prevent interference with the OS disk. If a VM fails, you can create a new OS disk with the same data disk, which ensures resilience and fault isolation. For more information, see Ephemeral OS disks.

document.name: wafsg-InRedundancyOptionsRedundancyChoices
document.title: Make VMs and their dependencies redundant across zones. If a VM fails, the workload should continue to function because of redundancy. Include dependencies in your redundancy choices. For example, use the built-in redundancy options that are available with disks. Use zone-redundant IPs to ensure data availability and high uptime.

document.name: wafsg-MaximumLoadExtraCapacity
document.title: Rightsize the VMs and their dependencies. Understand your VM's expected work to ensure it's not undersized and can handle the maximum load. Have extra capacity to mitigate failures.

document.name: wafsg-OneFaultDomainManyFaultDomains
document.title: (Scale set) Allow Flexible orchestration to spread the VM instances across as many fault domains as possible.
document.description: This option isolates fault domains. During maintenance periods, when one fault domain is updated, VM instances are available in the other fault domains.

document.name: wafsg-PreferredRepairActionPrematureRepairOperations
document.title: (VMs) Implement heath endpoints that emit instance health statuses on VMs.  (Scale set) Enable automatic repairs on the scale set by specifying the preferred repair action.  Consider setting a time frame during which automatic repairs pause if the VM's state changes.
document.description: Maintain availability even if an instance is deemed unhealthy. Automatic repairs initiate recovery by replacing the faulty instance. Setting a time window can prevent inadvertent or premature repair operations.

document.name: wafsg-ReliabilityDesignChoicesApplicationVmPatches
document.title: Run operations with rigor. Reliability design choices must be supported by effective operations based on the principles of monitoring, resiliency testing in production, automated application VM patches and upgrades, and consistency of deployments. For operational guidance, see Operational Excellence.

document.name: wafsg-ScaleSetDeploymentTimes
document.title: (Scale set) Enable overprovisioning on scale sets.
document.description: Overprovisioning reduces deployment times and has a cost benefit because the extra VMs aren't billed.

document.name: wafsg-TheVmInstancesScaleSet
document.title: (Scale set) Deploy across availability zones on scale sets. Set up at least two instances in each zone. Zone balancing equally spreads the instances across zones.
document.description: The VM instances are provisioned in physically separate locations within each Azure region that are tolerant to local failures.  Keep in mind that, depending on resource availability, there might be an uneven number of instances across zones. Zone balancing supports availability by making sure that, if one zone is down, the other zones have sufficient instances.  Two instances in each zone provide a buffer during upgrades.

document.name: wafsg-VirtualMachineScaleSetsFlexibleOrchestrationMode
document.title: (Scale set) Use Virtual Machine Scale Sets in Flexible orchestration mode to deploy VMs.
document.description: Future-proof your application for scaling and take advantage of the high availability guarantees that spread VMs across fault domains in a region or an availability zone.

document.name: wafsg-VirtualMachineScaleSetsServiceLevelDegradation
document.title: Be ready to scale up and scale out to prevent service level degradation and to avoid failures. Virtual Machine Scale Sets have autoscale capabilities that create new instances as required and distribute the load across multiple VMs and availability zones.

document.name: wafsg-VirtualMachinesQuotasDesignRestrictions
document.title: Review Virtual Machines quotas and limits that might pose design restrictions. VMs have specific limits and quotas, which vary based on the type of VM or the region. There might be subscription restrictions, such as the number of VMs per subscription or the number of cores per VM. If other workloads share your subscription, then your ability to consume data might be reduced.

document.name: revcl-EnhancedVmScaleSetsAutomaticInstanceRepairs
document.title: Enable automatic instance repairs for enhanced VM Scale Sets resiliency
document.description: Automatic instance repairs ensure that unhealthy instances are promptly identified and replaced, maintaining a set of healthy instances within your scale set.

document.name: revcl-PrivateRegistryRegionReplication
document.title: If using a private registry, configure region replication to store images in multiple regions

document.name: revcl-AgicAppgw
document.title: If using AGIC, do not share an AppGW across clusters

document.name: revcl-AksHttpRoutingAddApplicationRouting
document.title: Do not use AKS HTTP Routing Add-On, use instead the managed NGINX ingress with the application routing add-on.

queries.arg: where type=='microsoft.containerservice/managedclusters' | extend compliant = (isnull(properties.addonProfiles.httpApplicationRouting) or properties.addonProfiles.httpApplicationRouting.enabled==false) | distinct id,compliant

document.title: If required for AKS Windows workloads HostProcess containers can be used

document.name: revcl-AzureCniIpExhaustionDynamicAllocations
document.title: Use Dynamic allocations of IPs in order to avoid Azure CNI IP exhaustion

document.name: revcl-AzureNatGatewayEgressTraffic
document.title: Use Azure NAT Gateway as outboundType for scaling egress traffic

document.name: revcl-BestCniNetworkPluginAzureCni
document.title: Choose the best CNI network plugin for your requirements (Azure CNI recommended)

document.name: revcl-IngressControllerWebBasedApps
document.title: Use an ingress controller to expose web-based apps instead of exposing them with LoadBalancer-type services

document.name: revcl-ServiceIpAddressRangeClusterScalability
document.title: Size the service IP address range accordingly (it is going to limit the cluster scalability)

document.name: revcl-SlaBackedAksOffering
document.title: Use the SLA-backed AKS offering

document.name: revcl-StandardAlbBasicOne
document.title: Use the standard ALB (as opposed to the basic one)

document.name: revcl-UseDisruptionBudgetsDeploymentDefinitions
document.title: Use Disruption Budgets in your pod and deployment definitions

document.name: wafsg-AksUptimeSlaClusterArchitecture
document.title: Cluster architecture: Use the AKS Uptime SLA to meet availability targets for production workloads.

document.name: wafsg-ApplicationDeploymentManifestsPodResourceRequests
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Define Pod resource requests and limits in application deployment manifests, and enforce with Azure Policy.
document.description: Container CPU and memory resource limits are necessary to prevent resource exhaustion in your Kubernetes cluster.

document.name: wafsg-ClusterArchitectureCriticalWorkloads
document.title: Cluster architecture: For critical workloads, use availability zones for your AKS clusters.

document.name: wafsg-ContainerInsightsReliabilityImpactingEvents
document.title: Cluster architecture: Enable Container insights to monitor your cluster and configure alerts for reliability-impacting events.

document.name: wafsg-DifferentAzureRegionsInternetFacingWorkloads
document.title: Cluster architecture: Adopt a multiregion strategy by deploying AKS clusters deployed across different Azure regions to maximize availability and provide business continuity.
document.description: Internet facing workloads should leverage Azure Front Door or Azure Traffic Manager to route traffic globally across AKS clusters.

document.name: wafsg-ExtraManagementOverheadMemoryOptimizedVms
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Separate applications to dedicated node pools based on specific requirements.
document.description: Applications may share the same configuration and need GPU-enabled VMs, CPU or memory optimized VMs, or the ability to scale-to-zero. Avoid large number of node pools to reduce extra management overhead.

document.name: wafsg-IpAddressSpaceFailoverTraffic
document.title: Cluster architecture: Plan the IP address space to ensure your cluster can reliably scale, including handling of failover traffic in multi-cluster topologies.

document.name: wafsg-ManyConcurrentOutboundConnectionsAzureLoadBalancerLimitations
document.title: Cluster architecture: Use a NAT gateway for clusters that run workloads that make many concurrent outbound connections.
document.description: To avoid reliability issues with Azure Load Balancer limitations with high concurrent outbound traffic, us a NAT Gateway instead to support reliable egress traffic at scale.

document.name: wafsg-MatchingNodeSelectorWorkloadArchitectures
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Control pod scheduling using node selectors and affinity.
document.description: Allows the Kubernetes scheduler to logically isolate workloads by hardware in the node. Unlike tolerations, pods without a matching node selector can be scheduled on labeled nodes, which allows unused resources on the nodes to consume, but gives priority to pods that define the matching node selector. Use node affinity for more flexibility, which allows you to define what happens if the pod can't be matched with a node.

document.name: wafsg-RegularVmssBasedAksDeploymentSeparateDataCenters
document.title: Cluster architecture: Use availability zones to maximize resilience within an Azure region by distributing AKS agent nodes across physically separate data centers.
document.description: By spreading node pools across multiple zones, nodes in one node pool will continue running even if another zone has gone down. If colocality requirements exist, either a regular VMSS-based AKS deployment into a single zone or proximity placement groups can be used to minimize internode latency.

document.name: wafsg-TheAksUptimeSlaGuaranteesKubernetesApiServerEndpoint
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Use the AKS Uptime SLA for production grade clusters.
document.description: The AKS Uptime SLA guarantees: - `99.95%` availability of the Kubernetes API server endpoint for AKS Clusters that use Azure Availability Zones, or  - `99.9%` availability for AKS Clusters that don't use Azure Availability Zones.

document.name: wafsg-UserNodePoolsRightSizeSku
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Ensure your workload is running on user node pools and chose the right size SKU. At a minimum, include two nodes for user node pools and three nodes for the system node pool.

document.name: wafsg-UserNodePoolsSystemNodePool
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Keep the System node pool isolated from application workloads.
document.description: System node pools require a VM SKU of at least 2 vCPUs and 4 GB memory, but 4 vCPU or more is recommended. Reference System and user node pools for detailed requirements.

document.name: wafsg-WindowsBasedNodePoolsKubernetesNetworkPolicies
document.title: Cluster architecture: Ensure proper selection of network plugin based on network requirements and cluster sizing.
document.description: Azure CNI is required for specific scenarios, for example, Windows-based node pools, specific networking requirements and Kubernetes Network Policies. Reference Kubenet versus Azure CNI for more information.

document.name: wafsg-WorkloadArchitectureHorizontalScaling
document.title: Workload architecture: Ensure workloads are built to support horizontal scaling and report application readiness and health.

document.name: wafsg-WorkloadArchitecturesContainerInsights
document.title: Cluster and workload architectures: Configure monitoring of cluster with Container insights.
document.description: Container insights help monitor the health and performance of controllers, nodes, and containers that are available in Kubernetes through the Metrics API. Integration with Prometheus enables collection of application and workload metrics.

document.name: revcl-AdfPipelinesKeyVault
document.title: If using Keyvault integration, use SLA of Keyvault to understand your availablity
document.description: If your ADF Pipelines use Key Vault you don't have to do anything to replicate Key Vault. Key Vault is a managed service and Microsoft takes care of it for you

document.title: Protect logic apps from region failures with zone redundancy and availability zones

document.title: Select the right Logic App hosting plan based on your business & SLO requirements

document.name: revcl-AzureCosmosDbExtraProvisionedThroughput
document.title: Continous Backup with point-in-time restore in Azure Cosmos DB
document.description: Continous 7 day retention and 30 day retention backups. Azure Cosmos DB performs data backup in the background without consuming any extra provisioned throughput (RUs) or affecting the performance and availability of your database. Continuous backups are taken in every region where the account exists.

document.name: revcl-AzureCosmosDbRegularIntervals
document.title: Enable Automatic Backups
document.description: Azure Cosmos DB automatically takes backups of your data at regular intervals. The automatic backups are taken without affecting the performance or availability of the database operations. All the backups are stored separately in a storage service.

document.name: revcl-FtaResiliencyPlaybook
document.title: FTA Resiliency Playbook

document.name: revcl-LeverageAvailablityZonesOfcourse
document.title: Leverage Availablity Zones where regionally applicable and ofcourse if the service offers it

document.name: revcl-LeverageMultiRegionWritesMultiRegionWritesCapability
document.title: Leverage Multi-Region Writes
document.description: Multi-region writes capability allows you to take advantage of the provisioned throughput for your databases and containers across the globe

document.name: revcl-MaximumRetentionPeriodMinimumBackupInterval
document.title: Perform Periodic Backups
document.description: This mode is the default backup mode for all existing accounts. In this mode, backup is taken at a periodic interval and the data is restored by creating a request with the support team. In this mode, you configure a backup interval and retention for your account. The maximum retention period extends to a month. The minimum backup interval can be one hour.

document.name: revcl-MultipleReplicasDatabase
document.title: Run multiple replicas of the database (>1 ) in Prod

document.name: revcl-RegularBusinessContinuityDrillsAzureCosmosDb
document.title: Enable Service managed failover
document.description: Maintain business continuity during regional outages. Azure Cosmos DB supports service-managed failover during a regional outage. During a regional outage, Azure Cosmos DB continues to maintain its latency, availability, consistency, and throughput SLAs. To help make sure that your entire application is highly available, Azure Cosmos DB offers a manual failover API to simulate a regional outage. By using this API, you can carry out regular business continuity drills.

document.name: revcl-SeveralWellDefinedConsistencyModelsVariousConsistencyLevels
document.title: Choose from several well-defined consistency models
document.description: Choose from various consistency levels such as Eventual, Consistent Prefix, Session, Bounded Staleness and strong

document.name: revcl-SpanCosmosAccountData
document.title: Distribute your data globally
document.description: Span Cosmos account across two or more regions with multi-region writes

document.name: revcl-BusinessCriticalApplicationsActiveActiveConfiguration
document.title: For Business Critical Applications, use Active Active configuration
document.description: Should be used for DR configurations where an outage or loss of event data in the downed region cannot be tolerated. For these cases, follow the replication guidance and do not use the built-in geo-disaster recovery capability (active/passive). With Active/Active, Maintain multiple Event Hubs in different regions and namespaces, and events will be replicated between the hubs

document.name: revcl-DedicatedSkusPredicablePerformance
document.title: Use the Premium or Dedicated SKUs   for predicable performance

document.name: revcl-DesignResilientEventHubs
document.title: Design Resilient Event Hubs

document.name: revcl-GeoDisasterRecoveryActivePassiveConfiguration
document.title: Plan for Geo Disaster Recovery using Active Passive configuration
document.description: The built-in geo-disaster recovery feature, when enabled, ensures that the entire configuration of anamespace (Event Hubs, Consumer Groups and settings) is continuously replicated from a primary namespace to a secondary namespace, and it allows a once-only failover move from the primary to the secondary at any time. Active/Passive feature is designed to make it easier to recover from and abandon a failed Azure region without having to change application configurations

document.name: revcl-LeverageFtaResillencyHandbook
document.title: Leverage FTA Resillency HandBook

document.name: revcl-NewEhNamespaceLeverageAvailabilityZones
document.title: Leverage Availability Zones if regionally applicable
document.description: This will be turned on automatically for a new EH namespace created from the portal with Premium, Dedicated, or Standard SKUs in a zone-enabled region. Both the EH metadata and the event data itself are replicated across zones

document.name: revcl-AccessPolicyKeyVault
document.title: During failover, access policy or firewall configurations and settings can't be changed. The key vault will be in read-only mode during failover. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's failover guidance.

document.name: revcl-BackupLimitationsPastVersions
document.title: Understand Key Vault's backup limitations. Key Vault does not support the ability to backup more than 500 past versions of a key, secret, or certificate object. Attempting to backup a key, secret, or certificate object may result in an error. It is not possible to delete previous versions of a key, secret, or certificate.

document.name: revcl-EntireKeyVaultSingleOperation
document.title: Key Vault doesn't currently provide a way to back up an entire key vault in a single operation and keys, secrets and certitificates must be backup indvidually. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's backup and restore guidance.

document.name: revcl-KeyVaultBestPractices
document.title: Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's best practices such as isolation recommendations, access control, data protection, backup, and logging.

document.name: revcl-KeyVaultManagedService
document.title: Key Vault is a managed service and Microsoft will handle the failover within and across region. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's availability and redundancy.

document.name: revcl-KeyVaultSameGeography
document.title: The contents of your key vault are replicated within the region and to a secondary region at least 150 miles away, but within the same geography to maintain high durability of your keys and secrets. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's data replication.

document.name: revcl-KeyVaultSoftDeletedResources
document.title: Key Vault's soft-deleted resources are retained for a set period of 90 calendar days. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's soft-delete guidance.

document.name: revcl-MaliciousDeletionKeyVault
document.title: If you want protection against accidental or malicious deletion of your secrets, configure soft-delete and purge protection features on your key vault.

document.name: revcl-OptionalKeyVaultBehaviorPurgeProtection
document.title: Purge protection is recommended when using keys for encryption to prevent data loss. Purge protection is an optional Key Vault behavior and is not enabled by default. Purge protection can only be enabled once soft-delete is enabled. It can be turned on via CLI, PowerShell or Portal.

document.name: revcl-SameAzureSubscriptionKeyVaultObject
document.title: When you back up a key vault object, such as a secret, key, or certificate, the backup operation will download the object as an encrypted blob. This blob can't be decrypted outside of Azure. To get usable data from this blob, you must restore the blob into a key vault within the same Azure subscription and Azure geography. Familiarize yourself with the Key Vault's backup and restore guidance.

document.name: revcl-ActiveHotStandbyConfigurationActiveHotConfiguration
document.title: For applications, which required only read during failure, create Active-Hot standby configuration
document.description: The Active-Hot configuration is similar to the Active-Active configuration in dual ingest, processing, and curation. While the standby cluster is online for ingestion, process, and curation, it isn't available to query. The standby cluster doesn't need to be in the same SKU as the primary cluster. It can be of a smaller SKU and scale, which may result in it being less performant. In a disaster scenario, users are redirected to the standby cluster, which can optionally be scaled up to increase performance.

document.name: revcl-ContinuousDataExportOverviewLeverageExternalTables
document.title: Leverage External Tables and Continuous data export overview to reduce costs
document.description: Using the correct approach to feed a datalake with cold data and having the Kusto query engine at your disposal at the same time, as in the short-term storage

document.name: revcl-DemandDataRecoveryClusterConfigurationDisasterRecoveryScenario
document.title: For applications, where cost is a concern and can withstand some downtime during failure, create on-demand data recovery cluster configuration
document.description: This solution offers the least resiliency (highest RPO and RTO), is the lowest in cost and highest in effort. In this configuration, there's no data recovery cluster. Configure continuous export of curated data (unless raw and intermediate data is also required) to a storage account that is configured GRS (Geo Redundant Storage). A data recovery cluster is spun up if there is a disaster recovery scenario. At that time, DDLs, configuration, policies, and processes are applied. Data is ingested from storage with the ingestion property kustoCreationTime to over-ride the ingestion time that defaults to system time.

document.name: revcl-IngestDataCluster
document.title: Ingest data into each cluster in parallel

document.name: revcl-LeaderFollowerClusterConfigurationOptionalFollowerCapability
document.title: To share data, explore Leader-follower cluster configuration
document.description: Azure Data Explorer provides an optional follower capability for a leader cluster to be followed by other follower clusters for read-only access to the leader's data and metadata. Changes in the leader, such as create, append, and drop are automatically synchronized to the follower. While the leaders could span Azure regions, the follower clusters should be hosted in the same region(s) as the leader. If the leader cluster is down or databases or tables are accidentally dropped, the follower clusters will lose access until access is recovered in the leader.

document.name: revcl-LeverageInfrastructureCluster
document.title: Be fully cognizant of what it takes to build a cluster from scratch. Leverage Infrastructure as a Code for your deployments

document.name: revcl-ManagementActivitiesNewTables
document.title: Replicate all management activities such as creating new tables or managing user roles on each cluster.

document.name: revcl-MultipleAzureDataExplorerClustersAzurePairedRegions
document.title: For critical application with no tolerance for outages, create Active-Active-Active (always-on) configuration
document.description: This configuration is also called 'always-on'. For critical application deployments with no tolerance for outages, you should use multiple Azure Data Explorer clusters across Azure paired regions.

document.name: revcl-ReleaseAutomationToolWrapDevops
document.title: Wrap DevOps and source control around all your code
document.description: All database objects, policies, and configurations should be persisted in source control so they can be released to the cluster from your release automation tool.

document.name: revcl-TwoAzurePairedRegionsEntireAzureRegion
document.title: To protect against regional failure, create Multiple independent clusters, preferably in two Azure Paired regions
document.description: Azure Data Explorer doesn't support automatic protection against the outage of an entire Azure region. This disruption can happen during a natural disaster, like an earthquake. If you require a solution for a disaster recovery situation, do the following steps to ensure business continuity. In these steps, you'll replicate your clusters, management, and data ingestion in two Azure paired regions.

document.name: revcl-TwoAzurePairedRegionsTwoPairedRegions
document.title: For critical applications, create Active-Active configuration in two paired regions
document.description: This configuration is identical to the active-active-active configuration, but only involves two Azure paired regions. Configure dual ingestion, processing, and curation. Users are routed to the nearest region. The cluster SKU must be the same across regions.

document.name: revcl-ValidationRoutinesDataPerspective
document.title: Design, develop, and implement validation routines to ensure all clusters are in-sync from a data perspective.

document.name: wafsg-AzureContainerRegistryAzureStorage
document.title: Recovery: Ensure you have a recovery strategy defined. Machine Learning doesn't have automatic failover. Therefore, you must design a strategy that encompasses the workspace and all its dependencies, such as Key Vault, Azure Storage, and Azure Container Registry.

document.name: wafsg-BusinessRequirementsComputeClusters
document.title: Business requirements: Select your use of compute clusters, compute instances, and externalized inference hosts based on reliability needs, considering service-level agreements (SLAs) as a factor.

document.name: wafsg-DedicatedVirtualMachineTierLowPriorityVirtualMachines
document.title: Use the Dedicated virtual machine tier for compute clusters: Use the Dedicated virtual machine tier for compute clusters for batch inferencing to ensure your batch job isn't preempted.
document.description: Low-priority virtual machines come at a reduced price but are preemptible. Clusters that use the Dedicated virtual machine tier aren't preempted.

document.name: wafsg-MachineLearningWorkloadsDifferentGeographicalAreas
document.title: Multi-region model deployment: For enhanced reliability and availability, consider a multi-region deployment environment when possible.
document.description: A multi-region deployment ensures that your Machine Learning workloads continue to run even if one region experiences an outage. Multi-region deployment improves load distribution across regions, potentially enhancing performance for users located in different geographical areas. For more information, see Failover for business continuity and disaster recovery.

document.name: wafsg-MachineLearningWorkspacesExploratoryWork
document.title: Resiliency: Segregate Machine Learning workspaces used for exploratory work from those used for production.

document.name: wafsg-MultiRegionDeploymentTopologyDatacenterFailure
document.title: Resiliency: Deploy models to environments that support availability zones, such as AKS. By ensuring deployments are distributed across availability zones, you're ensuring a deployment is available even in the event of a datacenter failure. For enhanced reliability and availability, consider a multi-region deployment topology.

document.name: wafsg-OnlineEndpointsReleaseStrategy
document.title: Resiliency: When using managed online endpoints for inferencing, use a release strategy such as blue-green deployments to minimize downtime and reduce the risk associated with deploying new versions.

document.name: wafsg-SelfHealingCapabilitiesCheckpointingFeatures
document.title: Recovery: Ensure you have self-healing capabilities, such as checkpointing features supported by Machine Learning, when training large models.

document.name: wafsg-SufficientComputeResourcePlanning
document.title: Resiliency: Ensure you have sufficient compute for both training and inferencing. Through resource planning, make sure your compute SKU and scale settings meet the requirements of your workload.

document.name: wafsg-TensorflowEstimatorClassModelTrainingResiliency
document.title: Model training resiliency: Use checkpointing features supported by Machine Learning including Azure Container for PyTorch, the TensorFlow Estimator class, or the Run object and the FileDataset class that support model checkpointing.
document.description: Model checkpointing periodically saves the state of your machine learning model during training, so that it can be restored in case of interruption, failure, or termination. For more information, see Boost checkpoint speed and reduce cost with Nebula.

document.name: revcl-ApplicationGatewayAvailabilityZones
document.title: Deploy Application Gateway across Availability Zones

queries.arg: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/applicationGateways' | extend compliant = (isnotnull(zones) and array_length(zones) > 1) | distinct id,compliant

document.name: revcl-MinimumAmountAutoscaling
document.title: Configure autoscaling with a minimum amount of instances of two.

queries.arg: resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/applicationGateways' | extend compliant = (isnotnull(properties.autoscaleConfiguration) and properties.autoscaleConfiguration.minCapacity >= 2) | distinct id,compliant

document.name: wafsg-ApplicationGatewayBackendPool
document.title: Plan for rule updates
document.description: Plan enough time for updates before accessing Application Gateway or making further changes. For example, removing servers from backend pool might take some time because they have to drain existing connections.

document.name: wafsg-ApplicationGatewayInstanceShortTransientFailures
document.title: Review the impact of the interval and threshold settings on health probes
document.description: The health probe sends requests to the configured endpoint at a set interval. Also, there's a threshold of failed requests that will be tolerated before the backend is marked unhealthy. These numbers present a trade-off.- Setting a higher interval puts a higher load on your service. Each Application Gateway instance sends its own health probes, so 100 instances every 30 seconds means 100 requests per 30 seconds.- Setting a lower interval leaves more time before an outage is detected.- Setting a low unhealthy threshold might mean that short, transient failures might take down a backend. - Setting a high threshold it can take longer to take a backend out of rotation.

document.title: When using Azure Front Door and Application Gateway to protect `HTTP/S` applications, use WAF policies in Front Door and lock down Application Gateway to receive traffic only from Azure Front Door.
document.description: Certain scenarios can force you to implement rules specifically on Application Gateway. For example, if ModSec CRS 2.2.9, CRS 3.0 or CRS 3.1 rules are required, these rules can be only implemented on Application Gateway. Conversely, rate-limiting and geo-filtering are available only on Azure Front Door, not on AppGateway.

document.name: wafsg-DirectDependencyCallHealthEndpoints
document.title: Verify downstream dependencies through health endpoints
document.description: Suppose each backend has its own dependencies to ensure failures are isolated. For example, an application hosted behind Application Gateway might have multiple backends, each connected to a different database (replica). When such a dependency fails, the application might be working but won't return valid results. For that reason, the health endpoint should ideally validate all dependencies. Keep in mind that if each call to the health endpoint has a direct dependency call, that database would receive 100 queries every 30 seconds instead of 1. To avoid this, the health endpoint should cache the state of the dependencies for a short period of time.

document.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorBackEnd
document.title: Set a timeout on forwarding requests to the back end.  Adjust the timeout setting according to your endpoints' needs. If you don't, Azure Front Door might close the connection before the origin sends the response.  You can also lower the default timeout for Azure Front Door if all of your origins have a shorter timeout.  For more information, see Troubleshooting unresponsive requests.
document.description: Timeouts help prevent performance issues and availability issues by terminating requests that take longer than expected to complete.

document.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorFundamentalDeploymentApproaches
document.title: Choose your deployment strategy. The fundamental deployment approaches are active-active and active-passive. Active-active deployment means that multiple environments or stamps that run the workload serve traffic. Active-passive deployment means that only the primary region handles all traffic, but it fails over to the secondary region when necessary. In a multiregion deployment, stamps run in different regions for higher availability with a global load balancer, like Azure Front Door, that distributes traffic. Therefore, it's important to configure the load balancer for the appropriate deployment approach.

document.name: wafsg-AzureFrontDoorHealthProbesHealthEndpointMonitoringPattern

document.name: wafsg-FailureModeAnalysisAzureServiceLevelAgreements

For example, the SLO might be affected by the redundancy configuration that you chose. Consider the effect of a regional outage, the potential for data loss, and the time required to restore access after an outage. Also consider the availability of any internal dependencies that you identified as part of your failure mode analysis.

document.description: Redundancy protects your data against unexpected failures. document.name: wafsg-LastSynchronizationTimePropertyGzrsConfigurations-1
document.title: Before you initiate a failover or failback, check the value of the last synchronization time property to evaluate the potential for data loss. This recommendation applies only to GRS and GZRS configurations.
document.description: This property helps you estimate how much data you might lose if you initiate an account failover. All data and metadata that's written before the last synchronization time is available on the secondary region, but you might lose data and metadata that's written after the last synchronization time because it's not written to the secondary region.

document.title: Configure your storage account for redundancy. For maximum availability and durability, configure your account with zone-redundant storage (ZRS), GRS, or GZRS. Limited Azure regions support ZRS for standard and premium file shares. Only standard SMB accounts support GRS and GZRS. Premium SMB shares and NFS shares don't support GRS and GZRS. Azure Files doesn't support read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). If you configure a storage account to use RA-GRS or RA-GZRS, the file shares are configured and billed as GRS or GZRS.

document.name: wafsg-PremisesSmbFileSharesFileShareLevel
document.title: As a part of your backup and recovery strategy, enable soft delete and use snapshots for point-in-time restore. You can use Azure Backup to back up your SMB file shares. You can also use Azure File Sync to back up on-premises SMB file shares to an Azure file share.  Azure Backup also allows you to do a vaulted backup (preview) of Azure Files to protect your data from ransomware attacks or source data loss due to a malicious actor or rogue admin. By using vaulted backup, Azure Backup copies and stores data in the Recovery Services vault. This creates an offsite copy of data that you can retain for up to 99 years. Azure Backup creates and manages the recovery points as per the schedule and retention defined in the backup policy. Learn more.
document.description: Soft delete works on a file share level to protect Azure file shares against accidental deletion. Point-in-time restore protects against accidental deletion or corruption because you can restore file shares to an earlier state. For more information, see Data protection overview.

Design your applications to properly handle outages, which reduces downtime for customers.

document.name: wafsg-SecondaryRegionPrimaryRegion

document.name: wafsg-TimeRestoreOptionsDataProtectionOverview
document.title: As a part of your backup and recovery strategy, enable the container soft delete, blob soft delete, versioning, and point-in-time restore options.
document.description: The soft delete option enables a storage account to recover deleted containers and blobs. The versioning option automatically tracks changes made to blobs. This option lets you restore a blob to a previous state.The point-in-time restore option protects against accidental blob deletion or corruption and lets you restore block blob data to an earlier state. For more information, see Data protection overview.

document.name: wafsg-ApplicationRequestRoutingOtherHealthyNodes
document.title: (App Service) Consider disabling the application request routing (ARR) affinity feature. ARR affinity creates sticky sessions that redirect users to the node that handled their previous requests.
document.description: Incoming requests are evenly distributed across all available nodes when you disable ARR affinity. Evenly distributed requests prevent traffic from overwhelming any single node. Requests can be seamlessly redirected to other healthy nodes if a node is unavailable.  Avoid session affinity to ensure that your App Service instance remains stateless. A stateless App Service reduces complexity and ensures consistent behavior across nodes.  Remove sticky sessions so that App Service can add or remove instances to scale horizontally.

document.name: wafsg-AppServicePlanOverviewPremiumAppServicePlan

document.description: A premium App Service plan offers advanced scaling features and ensures redundancy if failures occur.

document.name: wafsg-AppServicePlanUserFlowDesign

document.name: wafsg-AppServicePlanZoneRedundancy
document.title: (App Service plan) Enable zone redundancy. Consider provisioning more than three instances to enhance fault tolerance.  Check regional support for zone redundancy because not all regions offer this feature.
document.description: Your application can withstand failures in a single zone when multiple instances are spread across zones. Traffic automatically shifts to healthy instances in other zones and maintains application reliability if one zone is unavailable.

document.name: wafsg-AutomatedRecoveryOperationsConductReliabilityTesting

document.name: wafsg-AutomaticHealingCapabilitiesAutomaticRepair
document.title: Plan your recoverability: Redundancy is crucial for business continuity. Fail over to another instance if one instance is unreachable. Explore automatic healing capabilities in App Service, such as automatic repair of instances.

document.name: wafsg-AutomaticProactiveMaintenanceAutomaticHealingRules
document.title: (App Service) Define automatic healing rules based on request count, slow requests, memory limits, and other indicators that are part of your performance baseline. Consider this configuration as part of your scaling strategy.
document.description: Automatic healing rules help your application recover automatically from unexpected problems. The configured rules trigger healing actions when thresholds are breached.  Automatic healing enables automatic proactive maintenance.

document.name: wafsg-AvailabilityZonesFaultTolerance
document.title: Build redundancy: Build redundancy in the application and supporting infrastructure. Spread instances across availability zones to improve fault tolerance. Traffic is routed to other zones if one zone fails. Deploy your application across multiple regions to ensure that your app remains available, even if an entire region experiences an outage.

document.description: Health checks can detect problems early. Then the system can automatically take corrective actions when a health check request fails.  The load balancer routes traffic away from unhealthy instances, which directs users to healthy nodes.

document.name: wafsg-HealthProbesUnresponsiveWorkers
document.title: Use health probes to identify unresponsive workers: App Service has built-in capabilities that periodically ping a specific path of your web application. Unresponsive instances are removed from the load balancer and replaced with a new instance.

document.name: wafsg-ReliableScalingStrategyRightScalingApproach
document.title: Have a reliable scaling strategy: Unexpected load on an application can make it unreliable. Consider the right scaling approach based on your workload characteristics. You can sometimes scale up to handle the load. However, if the load continues to increase, scale out to new instances. Prefer automatic scaling over manual approaches. Always maintain a buffer of extra capacity during scaling operations to prevent performance degradation.
